payload.title: What Are the Indonesian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
payload.excerpt: Indonesian wedding traditions by community, from Javanese siraman to the Batak ulos, plus what Australians should know about marrying legally in Bali.
key_takeaways: Javanese weddings run as a sequence across more than one day, from the siraman bath and midodareni night to the vow and the panggih meeting.
A Balinese Hindu wedding is a sacred rite of purification, so its ceremonies belong with a priest and the family, not on a reception programme.
Batik, the Minangkabau suntiang and the Batak ulos each carry meaning for a specific community and are best worn or given with that family's guidance.
To marry legally in Indonesia, Australians need a Certificate of No Impediment, a shared recognised religion and proper registration, so check every step with the embassy and the registry.

faq.q: Are you legally married in Australia if you get married in Bali?
faq.a: Generally yes, if the marriage was legally performed in Indonesia and would have been legal in Australia. That means the right religious ceremony and, for non-Muslim couples, registration with the Civil Registry. You cannot register the marriage in Australia, so keep your Indonesian documents safe.

faq.q: What do I wear to an Indonesian wedding as a guest?
faq.a: Ask the couple. Batik is a safe and welcome choice, and UNESCO's batik listing itself links the cloth to celebrations of marriage. Beyond that, dress modestly and follow the couple's lead.

faq.q: What happens at a Javanese wedding?
faq.a: In the palace account it unfolds in stages: siraman, the purifying bath; midodareni, the night before; the akad nikah vow for Muslim couples; then panggih, when the couple meet, exchange betel leaves and the bride washes the groom's feet. Families adapt it to their own region.

faq.q: Can non-Indonesian couples include Indonesian customs in their wedding?
faq.a: Yes, with care. Choose customs you have been invited into, keep sacred rites with their priests and families, and favour forms meant for celebration, such as batik or a dance performed for audiences.
